analysis.one_liner: Bars used-car dealers from selling, leasing, or loaning vehicles with unfixed safety recalls.
analysis.headline: The bill to force dealers to fix used-car safety recalls before sale died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing or a vote, ending with just 2 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made used-car dealers complete any open federal safety recall before selling, leasing, or loaning a vehicle. It covered anyone who sells ten or more vehicles to consumers a year, so it reached dealerships and rental-car sellers but not private individuals selling their own cars. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Used-car buyers, lessees, and renters, who would no longer be handed a vehicle with a known, unfixed safety defect, and everyone else on the road who shares the highway with those vehicles. The rule would have applied to commercial sellers — anyone who sold ten or more vehicles to consumers in the past year — while leaving private-party sales alone.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Used-car buyers and everyone on the road

how_it_helps.text: Prohibited a dealer from selling, leasing, or loaning a used vehicle until any defect or federal safety-standard noncompliance subject to a recall has been remedied.

Reached commercial sellers of any size above a floor: the definition covers any person who sold at least 10 vehicles to consumers in the previous 12 months, so dealerships, rental companies reselling fleets, and high-volume flippers were all covered, while a private individual selling one car was not.

Included narrow, practical exceptions: the ban did not apply if recall information was genuinely unavailable at the time of sale (not on the federal lookup system or the manufacturer's website), or if a court set aside the government's recall order; the Secretary could also exempt dealer-to-dealer auctions by rule, as long as the exemption did not harm public safety. The bill took effect 18 months after enactment to give sellers time to adjust.

analysis.who_pays: Used-car dealers, rental-car companies retiring fleets, and other volume sellers. The actual recall repair is typically performed at no charge by the manufacturer's dealerships, so the cost to sellers is mainly verifying recall status, holding vehicles until parts and repair appointments come through, and lost sales in the meantime — some of which would likely be passed into used-car prices. Auto manufacturers would also complete more recall repairs, which they generally fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: Used-car dealers and rental fleet sellers

drawbacks.text: The ban is absolute once a recall is known, even when repair parts are on backorder — a vehicle could sit unsellable for months, shrinking used-car supply and pushing some of the cost into prices for buyers.
The definition leaves a loophole: a person selling fewer than 10 vehicles a year — including small-scale curbstoners who flip cars for profit — falls outside the ban entirely.

The bill let the Transportation Department exempt dealer-to-dealer auctions from the ban by rule, a door that could have let unrepaired vehicles flow back onto retail lots, though only if the agency found the exemption would not harm public safety.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is cheap and targeted: buyers would know a vehicle they purchase, lease, or rent has no outstanding safety recall, and the repair itself is normally done free by manufacturers, so most of the burden on sellers is delay and paperwork rather than repair bills. The honest objections are the parts-backorder problem, the under-10-vehicles loophole, and the possible auction exemption — all design questions that could have been fixed in committee but never were, because the bill was never considered at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill on June 25, 2019, with Senator Edward Markey and one other Democrat as cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
That was the last action of any kind: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote ever appeared in the record for the remaining 18 months of the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Used-car dealers and rental-car companies that sell or rent vehicles with unfixed recalls are better off, because they can keep moving that inventory without completing the repairs; buyers remain exposed to known safety defects in the used vehicles they purchase.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Used-car dealers and rental fleet sellers

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on June 25, 2019.

against.name: Roger Wicker
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on the day of introduction and never reported it out, held a hearing, or scheduled a vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: National Automobile Dealers Association
against.role: Trade association for franchised car dealerships
against.what_they_did: Has publicly opposed federal and state requirements that dealers complete open recalls before used-vehicle sales, arguing that repair parts and manufacturer scheduling are not always available.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the only senators on record supporting the bill were three Democrats, and the Republican-chaired Commerce Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: Dealers would have to check every used vehicle for open recalls and hold it until the repair is done, adding inventory delays and compliance work; the bill's interest is directly the safety of the buyers they sell to.

The ban covers leasing and loaning as well as selling, so rental fleets with open recalls could not be rented out, and retired fleet vehicles could not be resold until repaired — a major channel for used-car supply.
More recalls would actually get completed, raising manufacturers' repair outlays, but completed recalls also cut their liability exposure and safety risk from defective vehicles left on the road.

The bill let the Transportation Secretary exempt dealer-to-dealer auctions from the ban by rule, potentially letting unrepaired vehicles pass through auctions back to retail lots, though only if the agency found no harm to public safety.
